title: Safari and the Great Migration
standfirst: How we build a East African safari for members: private conservancies, light aircraft, and a plan that follows the grass rather than a brochure.

blocks.heading: Two countries, one ecosystem, and a great deal of bad advice
paras: The aircraft drops onto a strip of red earth, the propeller winds down, and the only sound left is wind through grass. A vehicle is waiting in the shade of an acacia. Nobody checks a watch. That first quarter of an hour tells you most of what you need to know about whether a safari has been put together by someone who has been there.

The Mara and the Serengeti are one ecosystem divided by a border. The herds do not recognise it, which is why we plan across both countries rather than choosing between them, and why we are sceptical of any itinerary that sends members to the same three reserves regardless of month.

blocks.heading: Conservancies before parks
blocks.caption: A private conservancy: fewer vehicles, and permission to leave the road.
paras: The single decision that changes a safari most is where you sleep. National reserves cap nothing but your patience: vehicle numbers at a sighting are unlimited, you may not drive after dark, and you may not walk.

The private conservancies bordering the Mara work differently. Camps hold a fixed bed quota against a fixed acreage, so the number of vehicles that can reach any one sighting is small and known in advance. Night drives and walking safaris are permitted. The land is leased from Maasai landowners, so the money stays with the families whose grazing it is.
We place members in conservancies first and use the reserve itself as a day trip during the crossing season, rather than the other way round.

blocks.heading: What separates Kenya from Tanzania
blocks.caption: Short grass plains, where the herds calve between January and March.
paras: Kenya is the easier country to travel. Distances are shorter, light aircraft connections are frequent, and the conservancy model around the Mara is the most developed in Africa. It suits a first safari, a family, or anyone with ten days rather than three weeks.

Tanzania asks more and gives more. The Serengeti is roughly ten times the size of the Mara, the southern short-grass plains hold the calving herds early in the year, and the Ngorongoro Crater and Tarangire add landscapes Kenya cannot match. It rewards a longer trip and a higher tolerance for flying.

A member with a fortnight usually does both: Tanzania for scale and variety, Kenya for density and the crossings, joined by a single border-hop flight that we arrange rather than leaving to the camps.

blocks.heading: Camps that move with the herds
blocks.caption: Mobile camps are repositioned seasonally to stay with the herds.
paras: Permanent lodges are built where the view is good. Mobile camps are built where the animals are this month, then taken down and moved. For the migration that distinction matters more than thread count.

A well-run mobile camp holds six to ten tents, travels with its own guides and vehicles, and repositions three or four times a year. Standards are not compromised by the canvas: proper beds, hot water, a cook who has been with the camp for years.
Where a member wants the comfort of a permanent property, we pair it with a mobile camp for the middle of the trip rather than asking the whole itinerary to sit still.

blocks.heading: Bush, then ocean
blocks.caption: Balloon mornings are worth one day of the trip, not three.
paras: A safari is early mornings, dust and concentration. After eight or nine days of it most people want the opposite, and East Africa happens to keep the opposite a short flight away.

The Kenyan coast and the islands off Tanzania both work, and they are not interchangeable. The coast is quicker to reach and suits families. The islands are quieter, better for diving, and better for couples who want nothing on the schedule at all.
We treat the beach as the second half of one journey rather than a separate holiday, which means the flights, the laundry and the pace are planned as a single piece.

Every camp and conservancy we place a member in has been stayed in by someone on our side, and every guide is someone we can name. Where that is not true, we say so rather than filling the gap with a brochure.

blocks.heading: Timing the migration
blocks.caption: The river crossings, which peak in the weeks either side of September.
paras: The herds reach the Mara from the Serengeti from around July, and the river crossings that everyone pictures tend to peak between August and September before the animals turn south again in October. In the first quarter of the year the same herds are calving on the short-grass plains in southern Tanzania, which is a quieter and in some ways better spectacle.

The rains move these dates every year. We build flexibility into the middle of a trip rather than staking a fortnight on a single week, and we would rather tell a member their dates are wrong for what they want to see than sell them the trip anyway.

blocks.heading: Questions members ask before they commit
blocks.intro: East Africa rewards planning more than almost anywhere else we work. These come up nearly every time.

a: It depends on what you are going for. June to October is the dry season: grass is short, water is scarce, animals concentrate, and game viewing is at its most predictable. The crossings fall inside that window.
November to May is green, quiet and considerably better value, with superb birdlife and the calving herds in the south early in the year. The grass is taller and a few tracks suffer after heavy rain.

items.q: How do you move between reserves?
a: Light aircraft, almost always. Most legs are under an hour in a small bush plane, where the equivalent road journey would take most of a day. We hold the schedules ourselves rather than leaving connections to individual camps, so a delay in one place does not cost a night somewhere else.

At the right camps, yes. Several run proper programmes with tracking lessons and shorter drives, and some set a minimum age for standard game drives while offering family alternatives. We match the property to the children rather than assuming any camp will do.

Ten to fourteen nights is the usual shape: two safari locations so the landscape changes partway through, then four or five nights on the coast. Shorter is possible, but it means choosing between breadth and rest.

items.q: Can we have our own vehicle and guide?
a: Yes, wherever the property allows it, and we recommend it. It costs more. It also means you stay at a sighting as long as it deserves, leave when you want to, and plan each day around your own interest rather than a shared vehicle's.

items.q: What about the walking and the night drives?
a: Both are conservancy privileges rather than reserve ones, which is the main practical reason we favour conservancies. Walking is led by an armed guide and a Maasai tracker, usually early, and it changes the scale of the place entirely.

blocks.heading: We are ready when you are
paras: Every East African itinerary we build starts with a conversation about what you actually want from the days, and works backwards to camps, guides and timing from there.
